Yes, with people who I generally meet once a week at gatherings but don't really know that person well in person, I do learn a thing or two about them.

But, if you were to ask me if I really know and understand a person - then, 1. I never really tried to do that and 2. I don't think you can find out without reading too much into it and then again you are only seeing one side of the story as presented.

I ask this because it notably happened to me.

When I was in high school, stereotypically, I had a crush on a beautiful blonde cheerleader who was out of my league. I never did anything about it.

Skip ahead about 10 years. My then-girlfriend went to get her hair done one day, and when she came home, she said that the woman who did her hair went to my high school. It turns out that it was the younger sister of my crush. The then-girlfriend said she'd mentioned that her boyfriend went to that high school and then told her my name, and the younger sister said, "Really? You know - my sister had the biggest crush on him!"

Unsurprisingly, that tortured my soul for years. "If only..." I kept thinking.

Skip ahead again. A few years ago, at the urging of a friend, I set up a facebook account. I didn't much like the place, and never went back there. It just sat dormant for the last few years. About a month ago, there was a sudden flurry of activity on my account - apparently "I" had suddenly started joining all sorts of groups and posting all sorts of stuff, all on one topic. Naturally curious, I went to Facebook and discovered that my account had apparently been hijacked. So I reset the password and deleted all the posts and left all the groups and so on.

And I discovered - as long as whoever it was was there, they'd gone ahead and approved all of my pending friend requests. And one of them was from that long-ago crush. She'd apparently figured out who I was there and had sent a friend request, and now we were friends. And some of her posts were up on my page.

And I discovered, much to my ultimate relief, that she's loathsome. She's fat, bitter, shallow, self-involved and childish. So now, after all these years, I at last know that I didn't miss an opportunity - I dodged a bullet. And I have Facebook (and an account hijacker) to thank for that.

Like you I don't like Facebook at all, but my friends made me my account so I won't get rid of it. I only really use it for finding out info about various things that are going on (when and where the next party is etc.).

Here's my predicament. I have a scholarship to study Electrical Engineering. I am extremely interested in Computer Science. It's not that I'm not interested in EE, because I very much am, but I don't want to lose the scholarship. I'd like some input. Should I ditch the scholarship and study Computer Engineering (additionally, my school isn't yet accredited for CE specifically)? Or, should I double major? It would take a little bit longer, but it's certainly possible. What would be the career implications of this? Would potential employers look at my resume and think "Why on Earth did this guy go CS+EE instead of just CE?" I hope that I've made my concern clear and I am very appreciative for any input offered!
Computer Engineering vs. Comp Sci + Elec. Eng Degrees

Computer Science is problem solving using computers. Computer Engineering is building computers.

I wouldn't ditch the scholarship, because free money, but the job market for computer scientists is larger than that for computer engineers. Note I didn't say more lucrative, just larger.

"Why on Earth did this guy go CS+EE instead of just CE?"

I don't think anyone interested in hiring a CS or EE is going to ask that. If you're really ok with double majoring, I would do that.

This is exactly the sort of advice I was hoping to hear. I just hesitate because I hear so many people (including two profs) say "Well if you're interested in both EE and CS, just study CE." They don't understand that my situation is unique, though, and like you said, free money is good. Thanks for your help!

I have a CSE degree and, in my 15 year career, I have never once built a computer for work. That is not what CSE majors do, the degree is very versatile. It is a combination of electrical engineering curriculum and computer science, leaning more towards EE with a focus on the integration of the two fields.
Comp Sci + Elec. Eng Degrees = more money.

Would potential employers look at my resume and think "Why on Earth did this guy go CS+EE instead of just CE?"

No, most engineering employers see a double CS/EE major as a huge asset and generally see it as more valuable than a CSE degree. The combination is quite common and some schools even have an accelerated program designed to get both degrees in 4 years. Even so, people in the workforce with a combined expertise in both electrical engineering and computer science are rare and sought after. Especially if you choose a relevant concentration for your EE degree like robotics or control systems. With both degrees you will be able to work in many different industries and it will be much easier to switch industries if you desire. The need for custom software tools in engineering is universal and many groups are looking for people who can write/support their own and have engineering knowledge at the same time to better understand business needs and can do engineering work as well.
